READING THIS SCORECARD
Conformance and adherence come from the Audit Log - they prove the checks are happening, not just that breaks were found.
Findings per Audit rising with conformance steady usually means better detection, not worse performance - say so in the narrative.
A finding only counts as closed when the countermeasure is verified effective ~30 days after completion. Closed without verification is not closed.

QA GOVERNANCE - HOW TO USE THIS WORKBOOK
NOTS Logistics | Documentation standard for audits, breaks in process, containment & countermeasures

GOLDEN RULES: (1) Findings without audits behind them prove nothing - log every audit, including clean ones. (2) Contain first, countermeasure second. (3) "Retraining was completed" is a claim, not a countermeasure - document the steps and you have proof. (4) Nothing closes without a verification date.
The customer scorecard. KPIs vs editable targets with ON/OFF TARGET flags, 12-month trend, site and category breakdowns, countermeasure effectiveness. Only blue cells are typed.

One row per audit performed - even when nothing is found. Checkpoints audited vs conforming gives first-pass conformance; the plan-adherence block (right of the table) proves the audit cadence itself is being followed.
One row per finding, tied back to its Audit ID. Three gold columns must be complete: BREAK DETAIL, IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT, COUNTERMEASURE DETAIL.

THE LAYERED AUDIT CADENCE (adherence is measured on the Audit Log)
Daily quick checks against standard work in their own area. High frequency, few checkpoints. Default plan: 20/month per site.
Weekly structured observations across areas, including at least one process another lead audited - fresh eyes catch drift. Default plan: 4/month.
Monthly deep audit of one full process end-to-end, plus verification of a sample of previously closed findings. Default plan: 1/month.
Quarterly or as scheduled. Calibrates the site layers - if Layer 4 finds what Layers 1-3 missed, the finding is the audit program itself.
CONTAINMENT vs COUNTERMEASURE (never confuse the two)

Protects the customer from the defect that already exists: pull and re-verify suspect product, 100% re-check of work done by the same person/process since the last known-good point, stop-ship if needed, remove the EE from the process. Containment does NOT fix the cause - it stops the bleeding. Goes in the IMMEDIATE CONTAINMENT column.

Prevents the next defect from being created: retraining with verification, standard work change, visual control, error-proofing. Goes in the COUNTERMEASURE DETAIL column. A finding with containment but no countermeasure is still open, no matter how clean the product is.
THE COUNTERMEASURE ESCALATION LADDER (match the fix to the failure)

Weakest to strongest: Coaching -> Documented Retraining -> Standard Work Update -> Visual Control -> Error-Proofing / Poka-Yoke -> System-Enforced Control. Climb one rung automatically when: the same finding repeats, the same EE fails a second knowledge check, or the Countermeasure Effectiveness table shows a type running below 80%. A repeat finding answered with the same countermeasure is a red flag to any customer QA reviewer.
THE RETRAINING DOCUMENTATION STANDARD (5 steps - use this every time)
Remove the employee from the area where the error occurred. Record the date.
Give refresher training against the specific standard work document. Record the topic / doc number, the trainer, the date and the method (1:1, hands-on, group, LMS).

The TL or Supervisor monitors the employee for a defined period after the employee returns to the area. Record the start and end dates, how many observations were made, who made them, and how many errors occurred during monitoring.

The TL or Supervisor quizzes the employee on the correct process the following week. Record the date, who administered it, and the result. This is the step that separates real retraining from a signature on a form.

Record what happened next: - Passed: employee stated the process correctly and returned to normal unsupervised work. - Failed: employee could not state the process. Employee is removed from the area and assigned elsewhere to eliminate the possibility of another error, and the finding stays open.
WORKED EXAMPLE - INCORRECT KANBAN APPLIED DURING PICKING
EE placed the incorrect Kanban on a tote during the picking process.
Both affected totes pulled and re-verified before shipment; 100% re-check of the EE's work that shift; EE removed from picking pending retraining.

EE was removed from the picking area and refresher training was given. TL / Supervisor monitored the EE 6 times during the week following the EE's return to the picking area. EE was quizzed by the TL / Supervisor the following week on the correct process for applying Kanbans. Outcome 1 - EE was able to tell the TL / Supervisor what the process was and returned to normal unsupervised work. Outcome 2 - EE was not able to tell the TL / Supervisor what the process was. EE was removed from the picking area and assigned to another area to remove the possibility of another picking error.

Speaking to leadership about the depth of the retraining - by documenting the steps taken rather than simply stating that retraining happened - goes a long way toward proving that a soft countermeasure has a real chance of preventing recurrence.

Verification Due auto-fills 30 days after Actual Completion and turns red when missed. Verify by re-auditing the same process point - not by asking if it is fixed. Only then does the status become Closed - Verified Effective.

If the same break recurs after closure, reopen it: set the original to Closed - Ineffective / Reopened, log the new occurrence as a new finding marked Repeat = Yes, and escalate up the countermeasure ladder. Customers trust a log that shows reopened findings more than one that shows none.
Layer 1 audits logged same shift. Findings logged same shift, containment recorded before end of shift.
Supervisor reviews open findings, updates countermeasure detail, completes retraining documentation due, and closes the loop on any FAIL audits.

Set the reporting period on the Executive Summary, answer the four narrative questions, and issue the scorecard to the customer. Lead with conformance and adherence, then findings, then proof of closure - in that order.

Review the trend table and Countermeasure Effectiveness. Recurring 'Not Effective' results for a countermeasure type mean the fix is too soft for that failure mode - climb the ladder. Present the systemic actions taken, not just item-level closures.

During the picking process the EE placed the incorrect Kanban on a tote. Observed on 2 of 10 totes audited. EE pulled the Kanban from the staging rail rather than matching the card to the pick label on the tote, so the verification step in the standard work was skipped, not misread.
Standard Work PIK-04, Step 6: match Kanban part number to tote pick label and scan-verify before applying the card.

Both affected totes pulled from staging and re-verified before shipment. 100% re-check of all totes picked by the EE that shift (41 totes) - no additional errors found. EE removed from picking pending retraining.

Refresher training on PIK-04 delivered by TL M. Sanders 8/4 (hands-on demonstration of scan-verify). EE returned to picking 8/4 under monitoring: TL observed 6 pick cycles across the week of 8/4-8/8, zero errors. Supervisor quizzed EE 8/11 on the correct Kanban process - EE stated it correctly, including the scan-verify step, and returned to normal unsupervised work. Full step detail on Retraining Detail tab. Zero recurrence in the 30 days following.
Scan-verify step added to daily pre-shift huddle talking points for all pickers.

COUNTERMEASURE DETAIL - Narrative of retraining depth (this is what leadership reads)
EE placed the incorrect Kanban on a tote during the picking process - card pulled from the staging rail without matching it to the tote pick label. Scan-verify step (PIK-04 Step 6) was skipped.

EE was removed from the picking area on 8/3 and refresher training on PIK-04 was given by TL M. Sanders on 8/4, covering the match-and-scan verification step by hands-on demonstration. EE returned to the picking area 8/4 and the TL monitored the EE across 6 observed pick cycles during the week of 8/4-8/8; zero errors were observed. On 8/11 the Supervisor quizzed the EE on the correct process for applying Kanbans. The EE was able to state the process correctly, including the scan-verify step, and was returned to normal unsupervised work. Had the EE been unable to state the process, the EE would have been removed from the picking area and assigned to another area to eliminate the possibility of a second picking error. No recurrence at 30 or 60 days.
